chapters.title: Chapter 3: The Black-Scholes Formula, Step by Step

lessons.title: Put-Call Parity and Checking Your Black-Scholes Output

children.text: A Relationship That Doesn't Need Black-Scholes at All

Everything in this chapter so far has leaned on volatility, the normal distribution, and geometric Brownian motion. Put-call parity needs none of that. It is a pure no-arbitrage relationship between a call and a put sharing the same strike and expiry, and Chapter 1's replication logic is all it takes to derive it, with no formula, no σ, and no calculus anywhere.
Deriving It: A Portfolio That Always Pays ST − K
Build one portfolio: buy one call and sell one put, both struck at K, both expiring on the same date. Check what it pays at expiry in every possible outcome.

body.caption: Payoff of long call + short put, struck at K, at expiry

children.text: Every single row lands on the same combined payoff: ST − K, no matter where the stock ends up. That portfolio is not really an options position at all. It behaves exactly like a forward contract, a commitment to buy the stock at K on the expiry date, locked in today. And a forward's cost today is easy to pin down without any options math: buy the stock now for S0, and borrow the present value of K, K e^(−rT), to fund part of that purchase, repaying exactly K at expiry. The two sides of this equivalence must cost the same today, by the same law of one price from Lesson 1.3.

body.caption: Put-call parity. It holds for any correctly priced pair of European call and put with the same strike and expiry, regardless of which model, or which volatility assumption, was used to price either one.

children.text: Using Parity to Check Lesson 3.3's Answer

Lesson 3.3 priced an ATM Nifty call at ₹440.72, with S0 = K = 24,800, r = 6.5%, and one month to expiry, giving K e^(−rT) ≈ ₹24,666.03. Rearranging parity for the put: P = C − S0 + K e^(−rT) = 440.72 − 24,800 + 24,666.03 = 440.72 − 133.97 = ₹306.75.

Now check that against the direct put formula from Lesson 3.2, using the same d1 and d2 from Lesson 3.3: N(−d2) = 1 − 0.5500 = 0.4500, and N(−d1) = 1 − 0.5648 = 0.4352. P = K e^(−rT) N(−d2) − S0 N(−d1) = (24,666.03 × 0.4500) − (24,800 × 0.4352) = 11,099.71 − 10,792.96 = ₹306.75.

body.label: Two more roads, one more price
body.context: Parity, needing nothing but the call price and the risk-free rate, and the full put formula, needing σ and the whole normal-distribution machinery, land on the identical put price. This is the same "two roads, one price" pattern from Lesson 3.1, now confirmed a second time.

children.text: Why This Matters Beyond Checking Arithmetic

Three practical uses follow directly from this one equation. First, it is a built-in error check: if you ever build your own pricing spreadsheet or script, and your call and put prices for the same strike and expiry do not satisfy parity, you have a bug, no need to re-derive anything to know that. Second, it lets you find one price from the other without touching σ at all: if the call trades reliably but the put is thin and illiquid, parity gives you a defensible put price straight from the call. Third, it is the reason a long call plus a short put, at the same strike, is called a synthetic long stock position: the payoff table above shows exactly why holding that combination behaves like owning the underlying itself, funded partly on borrowed money, a structure traders actually build on NSE when it is cheaper or more convenient than buying the stock outright.

body.title: Apply parity to a fresh example
body.prompt: A one-month European call struck at ₹100 on a stock trading at ₹105 costs ₹8. The risk-free rate is 6% annually. Using put-call parity, what should the equivalent put cost, in rupees?

body.title: What parity does and doesn't need
body.question: You know a call's price, the spot price, the strike, the risk-free rate, and time to expiry, but you have no idea what volatility σ the market is using. Can you still find the matching put's price using put-call parity?
options: No, every options calculation needs σ somewhere
Yes, parity only needs C, S0, K, r, and T; σ never enters the equation
Only if σ happens to be low
body.explanation: Put-call parity, C − P = S0 − K e^(−rT), was derived purely from a no-arbitrage payoff argument. Unlike the full Black-Scholes formula, it never uses volatility at all, which is exactly why it works as an independent check on any σ-dependent calculation.

body.text: Put-call parity is Chapter 1's replication argument showing up one more time, in its purest form: a payoff that never depends on the outcome must have a price that never depends on a forecast, a model, or even a volatility estimate.

points: A long call plus a short put, same strike and expiry, always pays ST − K at expiry, regardless of outcome, exactly like a forward contract.
That equivalence gives put-call parity, C − P = S0 − K e^(−rT), derived from pure no-arbitrage logic without needing σ or any pricing model.
Applying parity to Lesson 3.3's ATM Nifty call (₹440.72) gives a put price of ₹306.75, which the direct put formula from Lesson 3.2 independently confirms.
Parity works as a built-in sanity check on any pricing tool, a way to price an illiquid put from a liquid call (or vice versa), and the logic behind synthetic long and short stock positions.
Unlike the full Black-Scholes formula, parity never requires a volatility estimate at all.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment advice. All prices, rates, and the stock example used here are hypothetical, built to demonstrate put-call parity, not to represent live market quotes.
